title: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
summary: Model an LLM reranker's tokens, calls, prefill and decode time per query; then cut them with single-token outputs, prefix caching, truncation, smaller lists, distilled 7B models and cascades.
outcomes: Compute calls, input tokens and output tokens per query for pointwise, listwise and pairwise LLM reranking
Estimate rerank latency from prefill throughput and time per output token, and find the critical path
Explain why single-token outputs like FIRST cut listwise latency more than shorter passages do
Apply prefix caching, truncation, smaller candidate lists and early exit, and name the quality risk of each
Compare a distilled 7B listwise reranker with a cross-encoder on compute and latency, and design a cascade

lessons.title: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases

blocks.md:
The prerequisite course showed how pointwise, pairwise and listwise LLM rerankers order a shortlist and how many calls each makes. This course is about the bill and the wait. A reranker sits on the query path, so every user query pays for it, and the p95 latency of search often becomes the p95 latency of the reranker.

Three quantities set both: how many calls a query needs, how many tokens each call reads, and how many tokens each call writes. We start with one call.

A rerank prompt has four parts: an instruction of $I$ tokens, the query of $q$ tokens, and $m$ passages of about $L$ tokens each (pointwise uses $m=1$, pairwise $m=2$, a listwise window $m=w$). The output is either one token (a yes or no label, a preference, a score) or a permutation of $m$ identifiers such as [3] > [1] > [2], which costs a few tokens per identifier.

blocks.tex: n_{\text{in}} = I + q + m\,L \qquad n_{\text{out}} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{label or score} \\ t_{\text{id}}\, m & \text{permutation} \end{cases}
blocks.caption: Tokens per call. t_id is the number of output tokens per identifier.

blocks.md: Serving an LLM call has two phases ([DistServe, Zhong et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.09670)). **Prefill** processes the whole prompt in one step and produces the first token; its duration is the *time to first token* (TTFT). **Decode** then generates one token per step; the average step is the *time per output token* (TPOT). DistServe notes that prefill of a non-trivial prompt tends to be compute-bound while decode is limited by GPU memory bandwidth, and that request latency is TTFT plus TPOT times the tokens generated after the first.

blocks.caption: Simplified model: P is prefill throughput in tokens per second. Ignores queueing, network time and fixed per-call overhead.

blocks.md: **Stated assumptions used in every number of this course** (illustrative, not measured): $I=100$, $q=20$, $L=100$ tokens, $t_{\text{id}}=3$ output tokens per identifier, a 7B model on one GPU with prefill throughput $P=8{,}000$ tokens/s and TPOT $=15$ ms. Swap in numbers you measure on your own stack.

blocks.title: One call of each kind, prefill versus decode

scenes.caption: Pointwise: 100 + 20 + 100 = 220 input tokens, prefill 220 / 8,000 s = 27.5 ms, and the one output token comes out of prefill. No decode steps.
Pairwise (PRP): two passages, 320 input tokens, prefill 40 ms, one output token. Still all prefill.
Listwise window of 20: 2,120 input tokens, prefill 265 ms. Then 60 output tokens for the permutation: 59 decode steps of 15 ms = 885 ms. Total 1,150 ms.
The surprise: in the listwise call, decode is 885 of 1,150 ms (77%) although it handles 60 tokens versus 2,120 read. Each output token is its own sequential step.

blocks.md: A sanity check against a real system: our window reads 2,120 tokens. RankGPT ([Sun et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.09542), Table 11) reports about 19,960 tokens over 10 requests per query when gpt-3.5-turbo reranks the top 100, about 2,000 per request. The same paper measured average API latency of about 1.1 s per gpt-3.5-turbo call and 3.2 s per gpt-4 call, so about 11 s and 32 s per query for its sequential windows.

blocks.prompt: Window call at the assumptions above (1,150 ms). Which helps more: halving passage length to $L=50$, or making the output a single token?
blocks.reveal: Halving $L$: input drops to 1,120 tokens, prefill to 140 ms, and the call to 140 + 885 = 1,025 ms, an 11% cut. A single output token: the call is just prefill, 265 ms, a 77% cut. Shorter inputs save money on every token billed; for latency in a decode-heavy call, the output length matters more.

blocks.md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

blocks.question: With the course assumptions, a prompt of 2,000 tokens produces 60 output tokens. Roughly how is the call time split?
options: About 250 ms prefill and 885 ms decode, so decode dominates
About 1,000 ms prefill and 135 ms decode, so prefill dominates
Equal, since every token costs the same time
Almost all decode, because prefill is processed token by token too
blocks.explain: Prefill: 2,000 / 8,000 s = 250 ms. Decode: 59 steps x 15 ms = 885 ms. Prefill processes the prompt in one parallel step; decode cannot.

blocks.question: You switch a pointwise reranker from a yes/no label to a short explanation plus label (about 40 output tokens). What happens to each call?
options: Only cost rises; latency is unchanged because input dominates
Latency per call rises by about 39 decode steps (about 585 ms here), far more than the 27.5 ms prefill
Latency falls because the model is more certain
Nothing changes if the calls run in parallel
blocks.explain: Each extra output token adds a TPOT step: 39 x 15 ms = 585 ms on top of a 27.5 ms prefill. Running calls in parallel does not shorten each call's own decode chain.

lessons.title: Calls and tokens per query for each method

blocks.md: Now multiply one call by the number of calls. With $k$ candidates: pointwise makes $k$ calls with one passage each. A listwise sliding window of size $w$ and step $s$ (RankGPT uses $w=20$, $s=10$) walks from the bottom of the list to the top. Pairwise Ranking Prompting (PRP, [Qin et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.17563)) asks each comparison in both orders, $u(q,d_1,d_2)$ and $u(q,d_2,d_1)$, to cancel position bias, so each comparison is 2 prompts.

blocks.tex: \begin{aligned} C_{\text{point}} &= k \\ C_{\text{list}} &= \left\lceil \tfrac{k-w}{s} \right\rceil + 1 \quad (k > w) \\ C_{\text{PRP-all}} &= k(k-1) \\ C_{\text{PRP-slide-}K} &= 2K(k-1) \end{aligned}
blocks.caption: Calls (prompts) per query. Multiply by n_in for input tokens.

blocks.md: For $k=100$, $w=20$, $s=10$ the formula gives 9 windows, starting at positions 80, 70, ..., 0; the [released RankGPT code](https://github.com/sunnweiwei/RankGPT) runs exactly that loop, while the paper's cost table reports 10 requests per query. PRP-Sorting uses heapsort as the comparator loop; its comparison count depends on the input order, so we counted it by simulation: 1,009 to 1,053 comparisons over 20 random orders of 100 items, mean 1,032, which is about 2,064 prompts.

blocks.title: Per query cost at k = 100 (course assumptions)

scenes.caption: Prompts per query: 100, 9, 1,980, about 2,064 and 9,900. Listwise makes the fewest calls by far.
Input tokens per query, in thousands: 22.0, 19.1, 633.6, 660.5 and 3,168. Pointwise and listwise read about the same; pairwise reads every passage dozens of times.
Output tokens per query: 100 for pointwise (one each), 540 for listwise (9 windows x 60), and one per PRP prompt: 1,980, 2,064, 9,900.

blocks.md: Why does listwise read about as much as pointwise despite 9 calls instead of 100? With $s = w/2$, each passage sits in about two windows, so input is roughly $2kL$ plus one instruction and query per window: $9 \times 2{,}120 = 19{,}080$ tokens. Pointwise reads $kL$ once but pays $I+q$ on every call: $100 \times 220 = 22{,}000$. The win of listwise is fewer calls (and fewer per-call overheads), not fewer passage tokens.

blocks.title: Input tokens per query versus candidates k

scenes.caption: Defaults (L = 100, w = 20): at k = 100, pointwise 22.0k, listwise 19.1k, cross-encoder 12.0k tokens. The listwise curve is a staircase: one more window every s = 10 candidates.
L = 300: pointwise 42.0k and listwise 55.1k. With long passages the double reading in overlapping windows outweighs pointwise's per-call overhead.
w = 40, step 20: 4 windows instead of 9, but input only drops from 19.1k to 16.5k. Each passage is still read about twice.
Cross-encoder tokens grow like k(q+L) too, but each token passes through a 22.7M-parameter model instead of 7B. Token counts alone hide that; lesson 6 compares compute.

blocks.md: Calls set the latency floor and the per-call overhead; tokens set the bill. Listwise minimizes calls, not tokens. PRP buys robustness to prompt order with 20 to 100 times more prompts than pointwise (220 to 1,100 times more than listwise) at k = 100.

blocks.question: You change RankGPT's window from w=20, s=10 to w=40, s=20 at k=100, L=100. Why do input tokens fall only from 19,080 to 16,480 although calls fall from 9 to 4?
options: The larger window tokenizes more efficiently
Larger windows truncate passages
The output permutation is shorter
Passages are still read about twice, since s = w/2; only the per-window instruction and query overhead is saved
blocks.explain: Input is about 2kL plus C(I+q). Only the C(I+q) term shrinks with fewer windows: 9 x 120 versus 4 x 120. RankGPT's own appendix (Table 12) also found larger windows did not raise nDCG@10 on DL19.

blocks.question: PRP all-pairs at k=100 issues how many prompts, counting both orders?
blocks.explain: k(k-1) = 100 x 99 = 9,900: every unordered pair (4,950) in both orders.

lessons.title: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count

blocks.md: Total tokens decide cost. Latency is decided by the **critical path**: the longest chain of calls where each needs the previous call's output. Listwise windows form a chain, because each window reorders the list the next window reads. Pointwise calls and PRP all-pairs calls are independent; the PRP paper notes all-pair calls can run in parallel. PRP sliding is a bubble-sort pass and heapsort's comparisons depend on earlier results, so both are chains.

blocks.tex: T_{\text{query}} = \sum_{\text{calls on the critical path}} T_{\text{call}}
blocks.caption: Independent calls overlap in time; dependent ones add up.

blocks.md: Parallel calls are only free when there is idle hardware. On one self-hosted GPU, prefill is compute-bound, and DistServe observes that once the GPU is compute-bound, adding requests to a batch stretches the batch time proportionally. So 100 pointwise prompts batched on one GPU take about total tokens / $P$ = 22,000 / 8,000 = 2.75 s, not 27.5 ms. Spread over 4 GPUs they take about 0.69 s. On a hosted API, concurrency is capped by your rate limits rather than by your GPUs.

blocks.title: Wall time per query at k = 100

scenes.caption: Listwise with generated permutations: 9 dependent windows of 1.15 s each, 10.35 s per query.
Pointwise on one GPU: 100 independent prompts, but one compute-bound GPU must still prefill 22,000 tokens: about 2.75 s.
Four GPUs split the pointwise prompts: about 0.69 s. More hardware shortens independent work; it cannot shorten the listwise chain, which still needs 9 steps.
Baseline: a MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder scores 1,800 docs/s on a V100 per its model card, so 100 candidates take about 0.056 s.

blocks.title: Latency per query versus candidates k

scenes.caption: Defaults: at k = 100, listwise 10.35 s, pointwise on one GPU 2.75 s, cross-encoder 0.056 s. Simplified: no queueing, no network time.
L = 300: listwise rises to 14.85 s and pointwise to 5.25 s. The cross-encoder line is held at the card's throughput; in reality longer passages slow it too.
w = 40: listwise falls only to 9.20 s. Fewer windows, but each window writes 120 output tokens, so the total decode steps barely change.
k = 200 roughly doubles everything: listwise 21.85 s (19 windows), pointwise 5.50 s, cross-encoder 0.11 s.

blocks.md: PRP chains are long. PRP-Sliding-10 at $k=100$ is 990 dependent comparisons; even with both orders of each pair in parallel at 40 ms each, that is about 39.6 s. Full heapsort is about 1,032 comparisons, about 41.3 s. All-pairs has no chain, so with enough hardware it can be fast, but it costs 3.17 million input tokens per query.

blocks.prompt: You get 10 GPUs instead of one. Which reranker's per-query latency improves the most: listwise sliding window or pointwise?
blocks.reveal: Pointwise: its 100 prompts are independent, so 22,000 prefill tokens split across 10 GPUs take about 0.28 s instead of 2.75 s. Listwise does not improve within one query: window 2 needs window 1's output, so 9 steps of 1.15 s remain. Extra GPUs raise listwise throughput (more queries at once), not its latency.

blocks.md: Parallelism is a latency lever, not a cost lever. Running 100 pointwise calls at once reads the same 22,000 tokens as running them one by one, and on a hosted API it uses up rate limits faster.

blocks.question: A team measures 10 s per query for RankGPT-style listwise reranking of the top 100 on a self-hosted 7B model. They double GPU count. What do you expect for a single query in isolation?
options: About 5 s, since work is split in half
About 20 s, from coordination overhead
About the same 10 s, since the 9 windows are a dependent chain
About 1 s, since all windows now run at once
blocks.explain: Each window reads the list as reordered by the previous window, so the windows cannot overlap within one query. More GPUs help when many queries run concurrently.

blocks.question: Which method has no dependent chain within one query?
options: PRP-Sliding-K
PRP with heapsort
Listwise sliding window
PRP all-pairs
blocks.explain: All-pairs enumerates every pair up front and aggregates win counts afterwards, so every call is independent. The price is k(k-1) prompts.

lessons.title: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking

blocks.md: Lesson 1 showed decode is about 77% of a generated listwise window in our model. FIRST ([Reddy et al. 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15657)) removes it. Instead of generating the whole sequence [5] > [1] > ..., it reads the logits (unnormalized scores over the vocabulary) at the **first** output position and ranks every candidate in the window by the logit of its identifier token. One forward pass, one token.

Why this can work: FIRST shows that RankZephyr, trained to generate full rankings, already has first-token logits that largely agree with the ranking it generates, while a pretrained LLM agrees considerably less. FIRST then fine-tunes Zephyr-beta (7B) with the usual language modeling loss plus a learning-to-rank loss (a weighted RankNet loss on the first-token logits) so the first-token logits are trained to order candidates, with more weight on the top ranks. Setup: top 100 Contriever candidates, sliding window $m=20$, step 10, as in RankGPT.

blocks.title: One window: generated permutation versus FIRST

scenes.caption: w = 20, L = 100: generation is 265 ms prefill plus 885 ms decode = 1,150 ms. FIRST stops after prefill: 265 ms.
w = 40: prefill grows to 515 ms for both. Generation adds 119 decode steps (1,785 ms), total 2,300 ms. The absolute gap grows with window size, as FIRST's latency figure shows.

blocks.title: Latency of one window versus window size

scenes.caption: L = 100: at m = 20, 1.150 s versus 0.265 s. The decode term (3m - 1) x 15 ms grows linearly with m and does not depend on L.
L = 300: at m = 20, 1.650 s versus 0.765 s. The gap is still 885 ms, but it is a smaller share, so the relative saving falls as passages get longer.

At m = 60 with L = 300, 4.95 s versus 2.27 s: the absolute gap keeps growing with m. Simplified: published FIRST uses single-letter identifiers A to Z, so windows above 26 need another identifier scheme.

blocks.md: What FIRST measured: on a 40GB A100, averaged over 200 sampled queries, it lowered reranking latency by about 50%, and the gap widened as the window grew. Holding latency fixed, FIRST could rerank more candidates than sequence generation and scored better on six BEIR datasets. Our toy model predicts a 77% cut per window because it has no fixed per-call cost, assumes 3 tokens per identifier and an assumed TPOT; FIRST also excluded the bracket tokens from the generation timing. The direction and the growth with $m$ match; the size depends on your stack.
Per query at $k=100$ in our model: 9 windows x 265 ms = 2.39 s for FIRST, versus 10.35 s with generation. The windows are still a dependent chain; FIRST shortens each link, not the number of links.
Output tokens are the expensive kind for latency. Prefer designs whose answer is one token or one logit: pointwise labels, PRP in scoring mode, or FIRST-style first-token ranking.

FIRST needs two things a plain chat API may not give you: logits over the identifier tokens at the first position, and a model whose first-token logits are trained or validated to rank well. With a zero-shot model, check that the logit order matches its generated order before trusting it.

blocks.question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
blocks.explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

blocks.question: Why does the relative saving of FIRST shrink when passages get longer?
options: Longer passages make the first-token logits less accurate
FIRST must generate more tokens for long passages
Prefill grows with L while the decode time saved stays the same, so the saved share falls
Long passages force smaller windows
blocks.explain: The saved part is (t_id m - 1) x TPOT, which does not depend on L. Prefill, which both methods pay, grows with mL.

lessons.title: Prefix caching, truncation and smaller candidate lists

blocks.md: With fewer output tokens, the remaining lever is input tokens. Three ways to read fewer of them: reuse work across calls (prefix caching), shorten what each passage contributes (truncation), and send fewer passages (smaller $k$, cascades, early exit).

**Prefix caching** stores the attention key and value tensors (the KV cache) of a prompt prefix and reuses them when a later request starts with the same tokens. In vLLM, [Automatic Prefix Caching](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/features/automatic_prefix_caching/) hashes each KV block together with every token before it, so a block is reused only if the whole prefix up to it matches; the [design notes](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/) say only full blocks are cached. SGLang's RadixAttention keeps prompt and output KV caches in a radix tree with LRU eviction and cache-aware scheduling. vLLM's docs are explicit about the limit: caching reduces prefill time, not decode time.

blocks.title: KV blocks reused across pointwise calls of one query

scenes.caption: Call 1 computes every block: instruction, query, then passage 1.
Call 2 starts with the same instruction and query, so those blocks hit the cache (green). Only passage 2 is prefilled.

Every later call reuses the shared prefix. At k = 100: 120 + 100 x 100 = 10,120 prefill tokens instead of 22,000, a 54% cut (simplified: vLLM caches only full KV blocks, so a few prefix tokens past the last full block are recomputed).
Bug: put the passage first and the query last. Now prompts differ from the first token, and no block can be reused.

blocks.md: Order the prompt from most shared to least shared: static instruction and any few-shot examples, then the query, then passages. Across queries only the instruction is shared, so long instructions and demonstrations benefit most. RankGPT's pointwise relevance generation with 4 in-context demonstrations was its most token-hungry method (52,970 tokens per query): exactly the shape where a cached demo prefix pays off. In listwise windows, only instruction and query repeat; the passages in a window change from the first passage on.

Hosted APIs offer the same idea. [Anthropic's prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) works with automatic caching or explicit cache breakpoints, has a default 5-minute lifetime refreshed on each use, bills cache reads at a fraction of the base input price and cache writes at a premium. [OpenAI's prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching) is on by default for supported models, needs the whole prefix to match, and bills cached input at a reduced rate. Both require a model-specific minimum prefix length, so a 120-token instruction plus query is usually too short to qualify; check the current docs for thresholds and rates.

**Truncation.** The RankGPT code cuts each passage to its first 300 words. Our model at $k=100$: $L=300$ means 55,080 input tokens and 14.85 s with generation; $L=100$ means 19,080 tokens and 10.35 s. **Smaller k.** At $k=30$ the window loop runs 2 windows (4,240 tokens, 2.30 s); at $k=20$, a single window. RankGPT used gpt-4 only on the top 30 after a gpt-3.5-turbo pass: 3,271 tokens and 1 request, versus 19,890 tokens and 10 requests to rerank the top 100 with gpt-4, about 16% of the tokens.

blocks.title: Listwise per query: passage length and candidate count

scenes.caption: Input tokens per query (thousands): 55.08, 19.08, 4.24, 2.12. Cutting k removes whole windows; cutting L thins every window.
Seconds per query with generated permutations: 14.85, 10.35, 2.30, 1.15. Truncation helps prefill only, so decode keeps the k = 100 rows slow.
Seconds per query with FIRST: 6.89, 2.39, 0.53, 0.27. With decode gone, both levers now act directly on latency.

blocks.md: **Early exit.** Search usually cares about the top 10. PRP-Sliding-K is itself an early exit: $K$ bubble passes fix the top $K$. A heapsort that only extracts the top 10 needs, in our simulation, 269 to 291 comparisons (mean 280) instead of about 1,032 for a full sort of 100. A listwise pass with $w=2s$ carries the best $s$ of each window upward, so one pass is already aimed at the top.

Every input saving has a quality price. Truncation can cut the sentence that made a passage relevant. A smaller $k$ means relevant documents retrieved at rank 31 or lower are never reranked. Measure NDCG@10 at each setting on your own queries before shipping the cheaper one.

blocks.question: You run pointwise reranking on a self-hosted model with prefix caching enabled, but see no cache hits. Your prompt is: passage, then query, then instruction. What is the fix?
options: Raise the cache size
Lower the temperature
Send the passages in a single batch
Put the instruction first, then the query, then the passage
blocks.explain: Prefix caching matches from the first token. With the passage first, every prompt differs immediately. Static instruction, then query, then passage makes the first 120 tokens identical across a query's calls.

blocks.question: Your listwise FIRST reranker at k=100 must drop from 2.39 s to under 1 s. Using the course model, which single change gets there?
options: Truncate passages from 100 to 50 tokens
Cut k to 30 (2 windows)
Enable prefix caching for instruction and query
Use a window of 40 with step 20
blocks.explain: k = 30 gives 2 windows x 265 ms = 0.53 s. Halving L gives 9 x 140 ms = 1.26 s. Caching the 120-token prefix saves under 0.15 s per window chain. w = 40 gives 2.06 s.

lessons.title: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design

blocks.md: Model size multiplies every token. **Distillation** trains a smaller model to imitate a large teacher's outputs. RankVicuna ([Pradeep et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15088)) fine-tuned 7B Vicuna on RankGPT-3.5 listwise orderings and matched zero-shot GPT-3.5 reranking on TREC DL19 and DL20, slightly behind GPT-4, with deterministic open weights. RankZephyr ([Pradeep et al. 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02724)) fine-tuned 7B Zephyr-beta on RankGPT-3.5 data, then on GPT-4 orderings for 5K queries, with variable window sizes and shuffled input orders; it closes the gap with RankGPT-4 and in a few cases goes beyond it.

Self-hosting a 7B reranker also unlocks the levers from earlier lessons: you control batching, you can enable prefix caching, and you can read logits, which FIRST needs. Note that the call and token counts do not change with distillation; the cost per token does.

The baseline to beat is a cross-encoder. The [MiniLM-L6-v2 cross-encoder](https://huggingface.co/cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2) has 22.7M parameters and its card lists NDCG@10 74.30 on TREC DL19 and 1,800 docs/s on a V100, so 100 candidates take about 56 ms. A forward pass costs about 2 FLOPs per non-embedding parameter per token ([Kaplan et al. 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361), ignoring attention). About half of MiniLM-L6's 22.7M parameters are its token embedding table, a lookup that costs no multiplies, leaving about 10.8M.

blocks.caption: Listwise 7B over the top 100 versus the MiniLM-L6 cross-encoder (about 10.8M non-embedding parameters) over 100 pairs of q + L = 120 tokens. Simplified: forward FLOPs only.

blocks.title: A cascade: cheap stages first, the LLM only where it pays

scenes.caption: Retrieval returns 100 candidates cheaply. Retrieval time is outside this course's model.
The cross-encoder scores all 100 in about 56 ms (1,800 docs/s on a V100, per its card).
Only the top 20 go to the 7B listwise model: one window of 2,120 tokens. With generated permutations that is 1,150 ms in our model.
With FIRST-style single-token ranking the window is 265 ms, so the cascade is about 321 ms of model time, versus 10.35 s for generated listwise over all 100.

blocks.md:
A practical order of levers, roughly from cheapest to most invasive:

1. Shorten the critical path: fewer dependent calls, parallel independent calls.
2. Shorten outputs: one label, one logit, or FIRST instead of a permutation.
3. Read fewer input tokens: smaller $k$, truncation, prefix-friendly prompt order.
4. Use a smaller model: a distilled 7B listwise reranker you can host.
5. Cascade: a cross-encoder narrows the list, the LLM orders the top few.

Write the cost model before choosing the method: calls on the critical path, input tokens, output tokens, and model size. Then check quality on your own queries: the cheapest design that holds your NDCG@10 wins.

Do not compare quality numbers across papers as if the setups matched. First-stage retrievers, candidate depth and datasets differ (RankGPT and PRP rerank BM25 top 100; FIRST reranks Contriever top 100). Re-measure on one pipeline.

blocks.question: Budget: 400 ms of model time per query, 100 retrieved candidates. Using the course model, which design fits?
options: Cross-encoder over 100, then a FIRST-style 7B on the top 20
Generated listwise with a 7B model over all 100
Pointwise 7B over all 100 on one GPU
PRP-Sliding-10 with a 7B model
blocks.explain: Cross-encoder 56 ms plus one 265 ms FIRST window is about 321 ms. The others: 10.35 s, 2.75 s and about 39.6 s.

blocks.question: RankZephyr is distilled into 7B from GPT-4 orderings. Which cost quantity does distillation change?
options: The number of windows per query
The input tokens per window
The compute per token, plus access to batching, caching and logits when self-hosted
The number of output tokens per window
blocks.explain: Calls and tokens follow from k, w, s and L. Distillation shrinks the model, so each token costs less compute, and hosting it yourself unlocks the serving levers.

blocks.question: Our estimate says the 7B listwise pass uses about 1,000 times the forward FLOPs of the MiniLM cross-encoder on the same 100 candidates. What is a valid reason to still use the LLM?
options: It reads fewer tokens
On your measured queries it ranks the top results better, and a cascade can limit it to a short list
Its calls are independent
FLOPs do not affect GPU time
blocks.explain: The LLM is used for quality, not efficiency. A cascade confines the expensive model to the few candidates where order matters most.
